paragraphs: This paper studies a bandit problem in which the expected reward follows a Bounded Mean Oscillation, or BMO, function. A bandit learner chooses among actions while learning about their rewards. Here, the reward function can have discontinuities and can be unbounded, allowing the problem to represent signals with singularities.

The authors develop mathematical tools and an algorithm for this setting. A central part of their approach is the performance criterion: delta-regret. Rather than comparing the learner with an unrestricted best action, this criterion uses an action that is optimal after a portion of the action space of size delta has been removed. That qualification matters when interpreting the guarantee.

The algorithm can achieve a polylogarithmic bound on this modified regret. The contribution therefore combines a broader class of reward functions with a carefully specified comparison target. It provides a way to analyze learning around irregular rewards, while its stated guarantee remains tied to delta-regret rather than ordinary regret against the unrestricted optimum.
icml-2020-bandits-for-bmo-functions-a639.tldr: The paper develops a bandit algorithm for discontinuous, potentially unbounded BMO rewards with a polylogarithmic delta-regret guarantee.

paragraphs: Medical monitoring devices produce repeated measurements of health indicators, creating an opportunity to update risk estimates as a person's readings change. This paper introduces BoXHED, a software package for estimating hazard functions from such data. A hazard describes the rate of an event occurring over time, making it useful for studying disease onset.

BoXHED uses gradient boosting with trees to implement an existing estimator designed for time-dependent covariates. These covariates are inputs whose values change during observation, such as monitored health readings. Its fully nonparametric approach allows the relationship between those inputs and hazard to be learned without prescribing a fixed parametric form. The contribution includes the first publicly available software implementation of that estimator.

Applied to cardiovascular disease data from the Framingham Heart Study, BoXHED reveals previously unreported interactions among established risk factors. The authors suggest these findings could resolve an open clinical question. That possibility is a qualified interpretation of the application, alongside the concrete contribution of accessible software for dynamic hazard estimation.
icml-2020-boxhed-boosted-exact-hazard-es.tldr: BoXHED uses tree-based gradient boosting to estimate changing health hazards from time-varying measurements.

paragraphs: This paper addresses structured stochastic convex optimization problems with many linear constraints. Such problems arise when combinatorial optimization tasks are converted into semidefinite programming relaxations. Even when the constraint count grows polynomially with problem dimension, repeatedly processing every constraint can make each optimization step expensive.

The authors propose two methods based on conditional gradients. Their defining feature is that an iteration processes only a subset of the constraints, avoiding the full passes required by the prior approaches discussed in the abstract. Both methods combine conditional gradient steps with variance reduction and smoothing. These ingredients support an optimization procedure that uses partial constraint information while still admitting a rigorous convergence analysis.

The paper provides convergence guarantees for the algorithms and preliminary numerical experiments illustrating their practical behavior. The main result is a framework that reduces constraint-processing work per iteration without abandoning theoretical analysis. The experiments offer an initial practical demonstration; the abstract presents them as preliminary evidence rather than an extensive evaluation across applications.
icml-2020-conditional-gradient-methods-f.tldr: Two conditional gradient methods process only subsets of linear constraints while retaining rigorous convergence guarantees.

paragraphs: Domain adaptation transfers knowledge between different data distributions. This paper focuses on cases where domains are organized by a continuous quantity rather than separate category labels. For example, patient age can index a range of medical prediction domains. Treating these as unrelated datasets overlooks the relationship expressed by the continuous index.

The proposed method combines adversarial adaptation with a discriminator that models the distribution of the domain index given an encoded representation. This makes the continuous index part of the adaptation machinery. The aim is to learn features that remain invariant across a range of domains while accounting for how those domains are related, rather than considering only categorical domain membership.

The theoretical analysis supports the value of using domain indices to obtain invariant features. Experiments on synthetic data and real medical datasets report better performance than the state-of-the-art adaptation methods used for comparison. Together, these results support treating continuous domain structure as useful information when designing transfer methods, with the empirical findings grounded in the evaluated datasets.
icml-2020-continuously-indexed-domain-ad.tldr: The method uses continuous domain indices, such as age, to learn transferable features across related data distributions.

paragraphs: In multi-label learning, a single example can belong to several categories at once. Many approaches assume the available labels stay fixed, but changing environments can introduce new labels over time. Deep Streaming Label Learning, or DSLL, addresses this setting by using knowledge from earlier labels and models to help learn newly emerging categories.

DSLL combines three components. A streaming label mapping learns relationships between old and new labels using a loss that accounts for label correlations. A feature distillation component transfers knowledge from a historical model into a new model at the representation level. A senior student network then learns the new labels with support from the accumulated knowledge.

The paper proves tight bounds on generalization error for new labels within its deep neural network framework. Its experiments also report significant improvements over existing state-of-the-art multi-label methods for continually emerging labels. The contribution is a coordinated approach to transferring both label relationships and learned features, supported by theoretical analysis and empirical comparisons in the changing-label setting.
icml-2020-deep-streaming-label-learning-.tldr: DSLL transfers knowledge from past labels and models to classify examples under continually emerging labels.

paragraphs: Neural processes use neural networks and latent variables to produce predictive distributions. This makes them promising for efficient prediction with uncertainty estimates. The paper examines a restriction of the standard formulation: it uses a global latent variable, even though some prediction problems also contain variation specific to individual targets.

The authors introduce the Doubly Stochastic Variational Neural Process, or DSVNP. Its prediction model combines a global latent variable with local latent variables. The global component represents shared variation, while the local components allow target-specific variation to enter the prediction. This hierarchical structure addresses the expressiveness limitation identified in models that rely only on a shared global variable.

Experiments demonstrate competitive prediction performance for regression with multiple outputs and competitive uncertainty estimation for classification. The results support using both shared and local latent structure when target-specific variation matters. The stated finding is competitive performance across these evaluated tasks, with the architectural contribution providing a more expressive way to organize latent information in neural processes.
icml-2020-doubly-stochastic-variational-.tldr: DSVNP combines global and target-specific latent variables to make neural process predictions more expressive.

paragraphs: POET generates learning challenges, develops solutions, and lets solutions switch between challenges to help escape local optima. This paper extends that approach toward open-ended learning: continually producing new, appropriately difficult opportunities. It identifies obstacles both inside the original algorithm and in the surrounding problem representation and evaluation methods.

Enhanced POET introduces two algorithmic changes. A domain-general measure evaluates how meaningfully novel a new challenge is, potentially supporting continued invention and solution of interesting problems. An efficient heuristic decides when agents should switch goals, helping the search scale. Two further changes broaden how environmental challenges are encoded and provide a generic measure of continued open-ended innovation.

The authors empirically validate these advances and report diverse, sophisticated behaviors across many environmental challenges, including many that other means could not solve in the demonstration. The work connects challenge generation, solution transfer, and progress measurement in one system. Its potential for endless invention remains a possibility enabled by the design, while the reported evidence demonstrates substantial open-ended behavior in the evaluated setting.
icml-2020-enhanced-poet-open-ended-reinf.tldr: Enhanced POET improves challenge novelty, goal switching, environment representation, and progress measurement for open-ended learning.

paragraphs: Few-shot object detection asks a model to detect rare object classes from very few examples. Although earlier work emphasized meta-learning, this paper studies a simple adaptation strategy: fine-tuning only the final layer of an existing detector on the rare classes. The authors find this choice crucial to strong performance in the task.

On the benchmarks they examine, the approach outperforms prior meta-learning methods and sometimes doubles their accuracy. The paper also identifies an evaluation problem: with so few training examples, the particular examples selected can cause large variation in results. A comparison based on one small sample can therefore give an unreliable picture of which method works better.

To improve reliability, the authors evaluate using multiple sampled groups of training examples and construct revised benchmarks from PASCAL VOC, COCO, and LVIS. Their fine-tuning approach also achieves state-of-the-art results under these revised protocols. The paper contributes both a strong, simple training strategy and an evaluation procedure that better accounts for variation in the few available examples.
icml-2020-frustratingly-simple-few-shot-.tldr: Fine-tuning only a detector's final layer performs strongly for rare classes, including under more reliable few-shot evaluations.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks must often handle inputs with different numbers of nodes and different structures. Pooling helps turn these variable inputs into representations suitable for graph classification or regression. This paper proposes HaarPooling, a pooling operation based on compressive Haar transforms and a sequence of clusterings of the input graph.

Each HaarPooling layer reduces the number of nodes while keeping the feature dimension unchanged. The transform removes fine detail in the Haar wavelet domain, producing a compressed representation. Applying these operations in a cascade eventually yields a feature vector of uniform size. The authors describe the transforms as providing a sparse characterization of the data while preserving information about graph structure.

Networks combining standard graph convolution layers with HaarPooling achieve state-of-the-art performance on the graph classification and regression problems evaluated. The contribution is a structured route from variable-sized graphs to fixed-sized representations. Its design makes graph clustering and the removal of fine-scale detail explicit parts of the pooling process, with empirical results supporting its usefulness across diverse tasks.
icml-2020-haar-graph-pooling-564a7f6b56.tldr: HaarPooling compresses graphs through clustered Haar transforms to produce fixed-sized representations while preserving structural information.

paragraphs: When learning agents communicate over limited bandwidth, they must choose both useful messages and useful connections. A communication protocol determines message content, while a scheduler helps determine who communicates with whom. This paper treats those choices together, since an informative message can still waste resources if the communication connection is unnecessary.

The proposed Informative Multi-Agent Communication method, or IMAC, draws on the information bottleneck principle to learn compact, valuable messages. The authors first establish a communication-theoretic result connecting bandwidth limits to the need for low-entropy messages during transmission. They then combine the learned protocol with a weight-based scheduler, addressing message content and communication allocation within the same method.

Experiments cover cooperative and competitive tasks with different numbers of agents and different bandwidths. IMAC converges faster and communicates efficiently under bandwidth limits compared with many baseline methods. These findings support jointly learning what to transmit and which connections to establish, with the information bottleneck supplying a principled motivation for keeping messages compact.
icml-2020-learning-efficient-multi-agent.tldr: IMAC jointly learns compact messages and communication scheduling to help agents coordinate under limited bandwidth.

paragraphs: This paper examines logistic regression when one outcome occurs much less often than the other. A dataset may contain enormous numbers of nonevents but relatively few events. The authors analyze how that imbalance affects parameter estimation, asking how much information the full dataset actually supplies and whether all its observations are worth processing.

Their asymptotic analysis shows that the maximum likelihood estimator's variance decreases at a rate governed by the number of events, rather than the total sample size. This places the available information on the scale of the rare class. They further prove that retaining only a small proportion of nonevents may yield an estimator with the same asymptotic distribution as the full-data estimator.

This gives a theoretical reason why undersampling nonevents may substantially reduce computation or data collection costs while preserving asymptotic estimation quality. The paper also studies duplicating event observations, a common oversampling practice. Besides increasing computation, that procedure may reduce parameter-estimation efficiency. Both conclusions are qualified: the results support possible advantages and losses, rather than universal outcomes for every sampling choice.
icml-2020-logistic-regression-for-massiv.tldr: For rare-event logistic regression, estimation information scales with event count, and undersampling nonevents may preserve asymptotic efficiency.

paragraphs: Face recognition depends on learning features that distinguish identities. Margin-based softmax losses are an important tool for this, but manually designing them requires exploring many possibilities. The paper also identifies a difficulty with an existing automated loss-search approach: its complicated and unstable search space can hinder the benefit of automatic search.

The authors analyze how reducing softmax probability relates to improving feature discrimination. Using that analysis, they construct a unified formulation for existing margin-based softmax losses. This formulation becomes the basis for a new search space. A reward-guided search method then automatically selects the best candidate within the search, connecting the design of candidate losses to the paper's analysis.

Experiments on multiple face recognition benchmarks show the method's effectiveness relative to state-of-the-art alternatives. The contribution lies in organizing the loss-design problem before automating the search. The results indicate that a search space informed by a common formulation of margin losses can produce useful objectives for learning discriminative face representations.
icml-2020-loss-function-search-for-face-.tldr: The paper unifies margin-based softmax losses and uses reward-guided search to select effective face recognition objectives.

paragraphs: This paper develops random fields for dependencies that vary across a domain and cannot be separated into independent component patterns. These properties matter in settings such as spatial and temporal modeling. The framework constructs such fields using an infinite mixture of convolved stochastic processes, providing different ways to control how dependence changes.

The authors distinguish two constructions. Stationary mixing combined with a nonstationary convolution function yields closed-form nonseparable kernels with constant nonseparability. Nonstationary mixing combined with a stationary convolution function instead produces varying nonseparability and better preservation of local structure. The distinction shows how assigning nonstationarity to different parts of the construction changes the resulting dependence patterns.

The fields also have interpretations through spectral representations of stochastic differential equations. Demonstrations span synthetic benchmarks and spatiotemporal applications in geostatistics and machine learning. The authors show that a single Gaussian process using these fields can outperform separable methods and existing nonstationary, nonseparable approaches, including treed and deep Gaussian processes, in both computational and statistical performance.
icml-2020-non-separable-non-stationary-r.tldr: Mixtures of convolved stochastic processes yield flexible random fields with constant or varying nonseparability.

paragraphs: Model-agnostic meta-learning, or MAML, learns a shared prior that supports adaptation across tasks. Its inner optimization adapts to each task, while its outer optimization improves the shared prior using performance across tasks. The outer objective is nonconvex, making it difficult to understand whether points reached by optimization are globally good solutions.

This paper characterizes the optimality gap of stationary points attained by MAML in both supervised learning and reinforcement learning. The analysis considers first-order optimization at both levels. It connects the gap from global optimality to two ingredients: the functional geometry of the individual task objectives and the representational capacity of the function approximators, including linear models and neural networks.

The authors report an analysis establishing global optimality for MAML with nonconvex meta-objectives. Its explanatory value comes from linking optimization quality to task structure and model expressiveness. The result should be understood through that characterization: it concerns the analyzed setting and its structural properties, rather than asserting that every practical MAML run necessarily finds a global optimum.
icml-2020-on-the-global-optimality-of-mo.tldr: The paper links MAML's stationary-point optimality to task geometry and model expressiveness, establishing global-optimality results for nonconvex meta-objectives.

paragraphs: A training example's usefulness can depend on what a model has already learned. This paper studies how to adapt the attention given to training data as learning progresses. Precisely measuring an example's eventual effect would typically require completing training first, making direct evaluation expensive when the scoring system must change alongside the model.

Differentiable Data Selection, or DDS, addresses this with a reinforcement learning approach that trains a scorer network together with the main model. Its reward favors examples whose gradients resemble gradients from a development set where good performance is desired. In plain terms, it increases the weight of training data that suggests parameter updates similar to those suggested by that development set.

Experiments on machine translation and image classification show strong, consistent improvements over several strong baselines without significant computing overhead. The findings support gradient similarity as a useful signal for adapting data usage during training. The development set has a central role: it supplies the reference for deciding which training examples deserve greater emphasis.
icml-2020-optimizing-data-usage-via-diff.tldr: DDS learns to weight training examples using gradient similarity with a development set, improving data usage during training.

paragraphs: Anytime neural networks produce a sequence of predictions that become more accurate as computation continues. Efficient designs reuse internal representations across these stages. This creates a training challenge: a representation must support a useful prediction immediately while also providing information that later stages can refine into a better answer.

The paper introduces Orthogonalized SGD, an optimizer that dynamically rebalances gradients associated with different tasks or outputs. For anytime networks, it projects gradients from later outputs into a parameter subspace that does not interfere with gradients from earlier outputs. This directly addresses the relationship between early prediction and later refinement when multiple outputs depend on shared parameters.

The authors study traditional branched architectures and introduce recursively nested networks. Experiments show significant improvements in the generalization accuracy of anytime networks trained with Orthogonalized SGD. The contribution combines architectural exploration with a training rule tailored to shared computation, showing that managing interactions between output-specific gradients can improve the predictions these networks make on unseen data.
icml-2020-orthogonalized-sgd-and-nested-.tldr: Orthogonalized SGD manages gradient interference between early and later predictions to improve anytime neural networks.

paragraphs: Distributed online learning involves local learners making predictions and exchanging information with neighbors. The paper starts from a projection-free conditional gradient method that handles complicated constraints with light local computation. Its drawback is communication: sharing gradients every prediction round requires O(T) communication over T rounds, despite an O(T^(3/4)) regret guarantee.

The proposed D-BOCG method groups the prediction rounds into sqrt(T) blocks of equal size. Learners update only at the start of each block, using iterative linear optimization steps. This arrangement retains the O(T^(3/4)) regret bound while reducing communication complexity to O(sqrt(T)). The central gain is therefore less frequent communication with the same stated order of regret.

The authors also extend the approach to bandit feedback, where a learner receives only a loss value rather than a gradient. They incorporate a classical one-point gradient estimator and obtain similar theoretical guarantees. The work shows how organizing updates into blocks can improve the communication requirements of constrained distributed learning, including under a more restricted feedback model.
icml-2020-projection-free-distributed-on.tldr: D-BOCG preserves an O(T^(3/4)) regret bound while reducing distributed communication from O(T) to O(sqrt(T)).

paragraphs: Roles can help organize a team of agents by encouraging similar behavior among agents with similar responsibilities. Traditional role-based methods define those responsibilities using domain knowledge. Multi-agent reinforcement learning offers more adaptability, but can be less efficient on complex tasks. ROMA brings these ideas together by allowing roles to emerge during learning.

The framework represents roles in a stochastic embedding space and conditions each agent's policy on its role. Two regularizers help shape that space. Agents with similar roles tend to share learning and specialize in particular subtasks, connecting the learned role representation to both behavior and how knowledge is shared across the team.

Experiments show that ROMA can learn roles that are specialized, dynamic, and identifiable. These roles help improve the state of the art on the StarCraft II micromanagement benchmark. The result supports learned role structure as a useful organizing principle for cooperative behavior, while the dynamic roles retain flexibility that would be restricted by fully predefined responsibilities.
icml-2020-roma-multi-agent-reinforcement.tldr: ROMA learns dynamic agent roles that encourage shared learning and specialization in multi-agent reinforcement learning.

paragraphs: This paper considers reinforcement learning when an agent must respect safety constraints that are initially unknown. The challenge is to learn about the environment and pursue reward while accounting for uncertainty about which behavior is safe. The proposed algorithm, SNO-MDP, separates learning the safety constraints from optimizing cumulative reward.

First, the agent learns about safety by expanding its safe region. It then optimizes reward within the region that has been certified safe. This step-wise design makes the learned safety boundary part of the reward optimization problem. The paper provides theoretical guarantees for satisfying the safety constraint and achieving near-optimal cumulative reward, explicitly under appropriate regularity assumptions.

The evaluation uses two experiments: synthetic data in the openly available GP-Safety-Gym environment and a simulation of Mars surface exploration based on real observation data. These experiments demonstrate the method's effectiveness in the tested settings. The theoretical contribution is conditional safety and reward assurance, with reward optimization carried out inside the certified safe region.
icml-2020-safe-reinforcement-learning-in.tldr: SNO-MDP learns a certified safe region before optimizing reward, with safety and near-optimality guarantees under regularity assumptions.

paragraphs: Tensor factorization represents interactions involving multiple entities through latent factors. This paper focuses on interaction events with timestamps, arguing that ignoring time or reducing it to coarse intervals loses useful information. It also identifies limitations in a previous event-based approach that captures excitation but omits inhibition and excludes dependencies beyond a local time window.

The proposed Bayesian model uses latent factors to construct mutually governed random point processes. These processes can represent events that encourage or suppress other events over both short and long timescales. A latent Gaussian process additionally models nonlinear relationships between entities that remain static. The factor representations therefore incorporate temporal influences alongside those static relationships.

For efficient inference, the authors derive a fully decomposed evidence lower bound that avoids a huge kernel matrix and costly sums inside event-rate calculations. They then develop stochastic optimization for the model. Results on four real-world applications show advantages for the method, supporting a representation that accounts for both excitation and inhibition across different timescales.
icml-2020-self-modulating-nonparametric-.tldr: The model factorizes timestamped interactions while capturing short- and long-term excitation, inhibition, and static nonlinear relationships.

paragraphs: Quantization represents a neural network's numerical values with fewer bits, supporting efficient deployment on resource-constrained devices. Many approaches preserve accuracy by using the full training dataset and additional fine-tuning. Post-training quantization avoids those requirements, but the paper describes existing simple optimization strategies as having mainly demonstrated effectiveness at eight-bit precision.

The authors propose Bit-Split and Stitching, a framework for pushing post-training quantization to lower bit widths with little accuracy loss. Its purpose is to make more aggressive numerical compression practical without fine-tuning the model. This addresses the tension between efficient deployment and preserving the behavior of the original, higher-precision network.

The framework is evaluated across image classification, object detection, and instance segmentation using various network architectures. The authors report that it can retain near-original performance even when converting 32-bit floating-point models to three-bit integer representations without fine-tuning. That finding establishes a demonstrated possibility across the evaluated work, rather than a guarantee that every model will retain its accuracy at three bits.
icml-2020-towards-accurate-post-training.tldr: Bit-Split and Stitching enables low-bit post-training quantization, with near-original performance demonstrated even at three bits without fine-tuning.

paragraphs: This paper explains contrastive representation learning through two geometric properties of learned features. Alignment means that features from positive pairs lie close together. Uniformity means that normalized features spread evenly across the hypersphere, the surface occupied by vectors of equal length. These properties describe both relationships between paired examples and the overall distribution of representations.

The authors prove that contrastive loss optimizes alignment and uniformity asymptotically, and analyze how these properties benefit downstream tasks. They also introduce an optimizable metric for each property. This turns the geometric explanation into quantities that can be measured during evaluation and used directly as learning objectives.

Experiments on standard vision and language datasets show strong agreement between the two metrics and downstream performance. Directly optimizing the metrics produces representations with comparable or better downstream results than contrastive learning in those experiments. The work thus provides both an asymptotic account of what contrastive loss encourages and empirical support for using those properties to guide representation learning.
icml-2020-understanding-contrastive-repr.tldr: Contrastive learning asymptotically promotes positive-pair alignment and uniform feature distributions, which can also serve as effective direct objectives.

paragraphs: A GAN's latent space can contain directions that correspond to understandable image changes, such as zooming or recoloring. Finding these directions gives users more control over generated images. The paper argues that discovery methods relying on labels, pretrained models, or self-supervision restrict the range of transformations they can uncover.

The authors introduce a model-agnostic procedure that discovers interpretable directions in a pretrained GAN without supervision or self-supervision. The GAN itself is already trained; the unsupervised contribution concerns finding useful directions within its latent space. The method identifies directions that produce meaningful semantic manipulations without requiring a supervision signal that specifies the transformation to discover.

One reported discovery is a direction corresponding to background removal, which the authors describe as difficult to obtain with existing methods. They use this finding to achieve competitive performance in weakly supervised saliency detection. This connects latent-space exploration to a practical image-analysis task, showing that a discovered control can be useful beyond manipulating generated images.
icml-2020-unsupervised-discovery-of-inte.tldr: An unsupervised procedure discovers meaningful controls in pretrained GANs, including a background-removal direction useful for saliency detection.

paragraphs: Sparse principal component analysis reduces dimensionality while restricting which variables participate in the representation. Finding a feasible solution does not by itself reveal how close that solution is to the best possible one. This paper focuses on that assessment problem, especially in the model-free setting, where the discussed existing methods lack efficient quality verification through dual bounds.

The authors propose a framework based on a convex integer program that obtains upper bounds in polynomial time. An upper bound gives a ceiling against which a candidate objective value can be compared. Their worst-case analysis relates the produced bounds to an affine function of the global optimum, providing a theoretical characterization of the bounds' quality.

The paper also reports that the framework scales more easily to large instances than a semidefinite relaxation approach. Numerical results on artificial and real cases demonstrate its advantages. The main contribution is therefore a way to assess solution quality through upper bounds, complementing methods that produce candidate sparse PCA solutions or converge to stationary points.
icml-2020-upper-bounds-for-model-free-ro.tldr: A convex integer programming framework supplies upper bounds that help assess the quality of model-free sparse PCA solutions.

paragraphs: Phase retrieval reconstructs a signal from its Fourier intensity, a problem arising in lensless imaging and imaging through scattering media. The paper describes complementary strengths and weaknesses in existing approaches. Conventional iterative methods show global convergence with clean data but struggle with noise, while previous neural approaches improve robustness yet can depend strongly on initialization.

The authors combine iterative phase retrieval with image statistics supplied by deep denoisers. They integrate these components through regularization-by-denoising, allowing learned information about images to influence reconstruction within an iterative algorithm. This design brings a learned image constraint into a conventional reconstruction procedure, rather than treating the two approaches as separate alternatives.

The resulting methods are reported to inherit advantages from both approaches and outperform other noise-robust phase retrieval algorithms. The finding supports hybrid imaging systems that combine established iterative methods with machine-learned constraints. The abstract's clean-data global convergence statement describes conventional methods; its reported result for the hybrid methods emphasizes their combined advantages and improved noise-robust performance.
icml-2020-when-deep-denoising-meets-iter.tldr: Combining iterative phase retrieval with deep denoisers improves reconstruction performance in the presence of noise.
